solution.concept_anchor: Regional metamorphism — orogenesis — high T and P; contact = heat only
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (contact metamorphism — mountain belts) is the strong distractor because students who know metamorphism occurs in mountain belts may associate contact metamorphism with such settings, not realising that mountain belt metamorphism is specifically regional, not contact.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): mountain belt metamorphism is regional (orogenic), not contact — contact is localized around igneous intrusions.
Eliminate option (c): dynamic metamorphism produces mylonite along fault zones, not hornfels — hornfels is the product of contact metamorphism.
Eliminate option (d): contact metamorphism involves heat only (from intrusion), not high pressure — the 'high pressure' component belongs to regional metamorphism.
Confirm option (a): Regional metamorphism — large-scale, high T + high P — associated with orogenesis (mountain building) — correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The UPSC trap is the conflation of 'metamorphism in mountain belts' with 'contact metamorphism.' Mountain belts are sites of regional metamorphism (both high T and high P over large areas due to crustal thickening during orogeny). Contact metamorphism is strictly localized — it occurs around igneous intrusions regardless of tectonic setting, and heat (not pressure) is its sole agent. Options (b), (c), and (d) each swap either the type, product, or agent of metamorphism between the three categories.
solution.final_explanation:
The three metamorphic types differ in scale, agent, and characteristic product.

• Option (a): Correctly matched. Regional metamorphism operates over vast crustal areas, driven by both high temperature and high pressure during orogenesis (mountain building). The Himalayan metamorphic core and Appalachian metamorphic belts are classic examples.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched. Mountain belt metamorphism is regional, not contact. Contact metamorphism is localised around igneous intrusions, independent of mountain-building scale.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched. Dynamic metamorphism produces mylonite (fine-grained, sheared fault rock) — not hornfels. Hornfels is the product of contact metamorphism (heat from igneous intrusions).
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. Contact metamorphism involves heat only (from nearby igneous intrusion) — pressure is NOT its characteristic agent. High pressure is the defining additional feature of regional metamorphism.

Value Addition:
• Index minerals for regional metamorphism: chlorite → biotite → garnet → staurolite → kyanite → sillimanite (Barrovian sequence).
• Hornfels is fine-grained, dense, non-foliated — formed when any rock type is baked by igneous heat.
• Mylonite's fine-grained texture results from mechanical grinding (cataclasis) along fault zones, not recrystallization from heat.

solution.concept_anchor: Diagenesis vs. metamorphism — temperature/pressure boundary
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is the strong distractor because both A and R are individually correct, and students who do not distinguish between diagenesis as the sedimentary-stage process versus metamorphism beginning at higher T/P may assume R automatically explains A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? Yes — diagenesis operates at low temperature and pressure (typically <200°C, <300 MPa) and is distinct from metamorphism which requires higher conditions.

Step 2: Is R correct? Yes — plate tectonics (subduction, collision) generates the high temperature and pressure conditions required for metamorphism, and diagenesis characteristically occurs before burial reaches metamorphic thresholds.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? No — R explains the conditions for metamorphism, not why diagenesis stops at low T/P. The reason diagenesis is distinct from metamorphism is the T/P threshold definition, not because plate tectonics drives metamorphism. R provides context but not the specific causal mechanism for A.
Both A and R correct, R does NOT specifically explain A → correct option is (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Diagenesis and metamorphism are both post-depositional rock-transformation processes, but they operate at fundamentally different temperature and pressure regimes.

• Assertion (A): Correct. Diagenesis encompasses all physical, chemical, and biological changes in sediment after deposition and before metamorphism — compaction, cementation, recrystallization at low T/P (generally below ~200°C and without significant directed pressure). It is categorically distinct from metamorphism.
• Reason (R): Correct as an independent fact — plate tectonic processes (subduction creating high P, collision causing crustal thickening and high T+P) are the primary drivers of metamorphic conditions in orogenic belts.
• Causal link: R does NOT specifically explain A. R describes what drives metamorphism, but it does not explain why diagenesis is limited to low T/P. The boundary between diagenesis and metamorphism is defined by mineral stability thresholds (e.g., appearance of zeolites, then chlorite marking the onset of metamorphism), not by the presence or absence of plate tectonics.

Value Addition:
• The diagenesis-metamorphism boundary is approximately 200°C and 300 MPa, where clay minerals begin recrystallizing into micas.
• Zeolite facies marks the lowest-grade metamorphism — transitional between diagenesis and true metamorphism.
• Oil and gas 'maturation' (conversion of organic matter to hydrocarbons) is a diagenetic process governed by temperature during burial.

solution.concept_anchor: Sill — concordant intrusive body — horizontal emplacement
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (laccolith) is the strong distractor because sills and laccoliths are both concordant intrusive bodies that run parallel to strata; students who know laccoliths form dome-shaped hills but cannot distinguish the flat-sheet geometry of a sill will select option (c).
elimination_logic: The intrusion runs parallel to sedimentary strata (concordant) — rules out dyke (discordant) and batholith (discordant/massive).
The exposed feature is a flat, sheet-like ledge — rules out laccolith, which domes up overlying strata into a hill.
A flat concordant sheet-like intrusion forming a ledge or stepped terrain after erosion = sill.
Answer is (b) sill.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both sills and laccoliths are concordant (parallel to strata), which is the shared attribute that makes laccoliths a compelling distractor here. The differentiating detail is morphology: sills are horizontal, sheet-like bodies of roughly uniform thickness that do not dome the overlying rock; laccoliths are fed from below and arch upward, doming overlying strata into a convex hill. The scenario's description of a 'flat ledge-like exposure' as opposed to a 'rounded dome' is the key discriminating phrase that separates the correct answer (sill) from the trap (laccolith).
solution.final_explanation:
Intrusive igneous bodies are identified by their geometric relationship to the host rock and their exposed morphology after denudation.

In the scenario: the intrusion is parallel to existing sedimentary strata (concordant), sheet-like and of uniform thickness, and its erosional exposure creates a flat stepped ledge — not a rounded dome. This precisely describes a sill.

• Option (a) — Dyke: Incorrect. Dykes cut across rock strata at an angle (discordant). The scenario specifies parallel emplacement.
• Option (b) — Sill: Correct. A sill is a concordant, sheet-like intrusion emplaced parallel to and between sedimentary layers. When resistant to erosion, it forms flat-topped ledges or stepped terrain — as described.
• Option (c) — Laccolith: Incorrect. Laccoliths are also concordant but mushroom-shaped — they arch overlying strata into a dome. The scenario's 'flat ledge' morphology excludes laccolith.
• Option (d) — Batholith: Incorrect. Batholiths are massive, discordant plutonic bodies forming the cores of mountain ranges — not sheet-like intrusions.

Value Addition:
• The Palisades Sill along the Hudson River (USA) is a classic example of a sill forming resistant cliffs.
• Sills can be mistaken for lava flows in the field — their intrusive origin is confirmed by baked (metamorphosed) contacts with surrounding rock.
• Multiple sills stacked vertically can contribute to the stepped topography of trap landscapes.

solution.concept_anchor: Anthracite highest rank — lignite lowest — frequently reversed in UPSC options

statement_analysis.statement: Anthracite is the highest rank coal with the greatest carbon content and lowest moisture and volatile matter content among all coal varieties.
statement_analysis.reason: Anthracite represents the most mature stage of coalification — it contains over 90% carbon, burns with a smokeless blue flame, and has minimal moisture and volatile matter. It is definitionally the highest-rank coal.

statement_analysis.statement: Lignite, being a low-rank coal with high volatile matter content, is found predominantly in the Gondwana sedimentary sequences of Peninsular India and provides the bulk of India's coal for steel production.
statement_analysis.reason: Lignite is found in Tertiary deposits (Assam, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu/Neyveli) — NOT in Gondwana sequences. Gondwana sequences (Permian) contain bituminous coal. Furthermore, coking coal for steel production comes from bituminous Gondwana fields (e.g., Jharia), not from lignite.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is the strong distractor because students who correctly know Statement 1 about anthracite and vaguely associate lignite with Indian coal without distinguishing Gondwana vs. Tertiary deposits will accept Statement 2 as true.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Anthracite = highest carbon, lowest moisture/volatiles — textbook definition, correct.
Examine Statement 2 part 1: Lignite in Gondwana sequences? No — Gondwana = Permian bituminous coal; lignite is in Tertiary sequences (Assam, Tamil Nadu).
Examine Statement 2 part 2: Lignite for steel production? No — coking coal (bituminous) is used in steel; lignite is used only for thermal power.
Statement 2 is incorrect on both counts → answer is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 plants a double error: geographic assignment (lignite to Gondwana sequences, which is wrong — Gondwana holds bituminous coal) and economic application (lignite for steel, which is wrong — only high-rank coking coal from Jharia/Gondwana fields is used in metallurgy). Students who have only broad knowledge of 'India has Gondwana coalfields' and 'lignite is low-grade coal' may not catch that lignite is specifically a Tertiary product, not Gondwana.
solution.final_explanation:
Coal rank and India's coal geography are two precision-critical dimensions that UPSC questions regularly probe.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Anthracite is the highest metamorphic (coalification) stage of coal. It has the highest fixed carbon (>90%), lowest moisture, and lowest volatile matter. Its near-complete coalification makes it the densest and hardest coal variety.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect on two counts: (1) Lignite is found in Tertiary sedimentary deposits — Neyveli (Tamil Nadu), Barmer (Rajasthan), and Assam — NOT in Gondwana sequences. Gondwana formations (Permian age) host bituminous and sub-bituminous coal. (2) Lignite cannot substitute for coking coal in steel production; steel requires high-grade coking (bituminous) coal from Jharia and other Gondwana fields.

Value Addition:
• Gondwana coalfields (Permian): Jharia, Bokaro, Raniganj, Talcher, Singareni — bituminous to high-volatile coking coal.
• Tertiary coalfields: Makum (Assam), Neyveli (Tamil Nadu) — lignite, used for thermal power.
• India has negligible anthracite reserves — most coal is sub-bituminous to bituminous grade.

solution.concept_anchor: Limestone karst secondary porosity — most productive aquifer type
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (shale aquifer) is the strong distractor because shale has very high total porosity (many tiny pores) and students confuse high porosity with high permeability, not realising shale's micropores prevent water flow, making it an aquitard.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): unweathered granite has very low primary porosity — poor aquifer unless fractured.
Eliminate option (b): shale has high porosity but very low permeability — water cannot move through it; it is an aquitard, not an aquifer.
Eliminate option (d): obsidian is volcanic glass with essentially no porosity or permeability.
Confirm option (c): limestone develops secondary porosity through dissolution (karst), forming highly productive aquifer systems globally.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The shale trap (option b) exploits the distinction between porosity and permeability — two terms students often conflate. Shale has high total porosity (many pores) but extremely low permeability (tiny, poorly connected pores that prevent water flow). It is the classic aquitard in confined aquifer systems. Limestone, by contrast, develops secondary porosity through dissolution (caves, fractures, conduits), creating highly transmissive karst aquifer systems.
solution.final_explanation:
Aquifer productivity depends on both porosity (storage) and permeability (transmission). Limestone stands out as a highly productive aquifer because of its secondary (karst) porosity.

• Option (a) — Unweathered granite: Poor aquifer. Low primary porosity. Only fractured/weathered granite develops useful secondary porosity for groundwater storage.
• Option (b) — Shale: Poor aquifer (aquitard). Despite high total porosity, shale's micropores are so small they prevent meaningful water flow (very low permeability). Shale forms impermeable confining layers in artesian systems.
• Option (c) — Limestone with karst development: Correct. Dissolution of calcite by carbonic acid creates caves, conduits, and fracture networks — secondary porosity of exceptional transmissivity. Karst aquifers are among the most productive globally.
• Option (d) — Obsidian: No porosity or permeability. Volcanic glass — solidified without any pore structure.

Value Addition:
• Primary porosity: formed during rock creation (intergranular spaces in sandstone).
• Secondary porosity: developed after formation (fractures in granite, dissolution voids in limestone).
• India's hard rock aquifer challenge: the Deccan plateau (basalt and granite) relies on secondary fracture porosity — highly variable and difficult to manage.

solution.concept_anchor: MORB at divergent boundaries — granite continental only

statement_analysis.statement: Mid-Ocean Ridge Basalt (MORB) is the most voluminous igneous rock on Earth by area, forming the oceanic crust at divergent plate boundaries through decompression melting of the mantle.
statement_analysis.reason: MORB covers approximately two-thirds of Earth's surface as oceanic crust. It forms at divergent boundaries where rising asthenosphere undergoes decompression melting without any addition of water — producing tholeiitic basalt.

statement_analysis.statement: Granite is the dominant rock type of both continental and oceanic crust, forming the structural foundation of all major tectonic plates.
statement_analysis.reason: Granite dominates continental crust; oceanic crust is basaltic (MORB). The claim that granite forms the foundation of all tectonic plates — including oceanic plates — is categorically false.

statement_analysis.statement: Andesitic volcanism characteristic of subduction zones results from the partial melting of the subducting slab and overlying mantle wedge, often with hydration from water released by the descending oceanic plate.
statement_analysis.reason: Water released from hydrated minerals in the subducting slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge, generating andesitic (intermediate silica) magma — the basis of 'Ring of Fire' volcanism.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is the strong distractor because statements 1 and 3 are both accurate and detailed, leading students who accept Statement 2's claim about granite without recalling the oceanic crust is basaltic to mark all three correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: MORB = most voluminous igneous rock, forms at divergent boundaries by decompression melting — correct.
Statement 2: Granite in BOTH continental and oceanic crust — FALSE. Oceanic crust = basaltic, not granitic. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: Andesite from subduction — hydration melting mechanism — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → answer is (a) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 targets students who know granite is a major igneous rock and extrapolate this to oceanic crust as well. The critical distinction is crustal type: continental crust is predominantly felsic (granite, granodiorite) while oceanic crust is uniformly mafic (basalt, gabbro). This crust-type compositional difference is fundamental to plate tectonics — subduction occurs where denser basaltic oceanic crust sinks beneath lighter granitic continental crust. Students without this precise distinction are the intended victims.
solution.final_explanation:
Plate tectonic settings produce distinct rock assemblages based on the dominant geological processes at each boundary type.

• Statement 1 — Correct: MORB forms at mid-ocean ridges by decompression melting — as the mantle rises toward the surface, pressure decreases and it melts without temperature increase. It constitutes the entire oceanic crust — roughly 70% of Earth's surface.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Granite is exclusively continental. Oceanic crust consists of basalt (upper) and gabbro (lower) — both mafic rocks crystallized from MORB-type magma. No granite is produced at mid-ocean ridges.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Subduction introduces water into the mantle wedge via dehydration of hydrous minerals (serpentinite, amphibole) in the descending slab. This water lowers the peridotite melting point, generating andesitic to rhyolitic magmas in arc volcanism.

Value Addition:
• The Mohorovičić discontinuity (Moho) separates crust from mantle — shallower under oceans (~7 km) than continents (~35 km).
• Island arcs (e.g., Japan, Philippines, Aleutians) are built on andesitic/basaltic volcanism from ocean-ocean subduction.
• Continental arcs (e.g., Andes) produce more silicic (andesite to rhyolite/dacite) volcanism because continental crust contaminates the magma.

solution.concept_anchor: Protolith-metamorphic product pairs including non-foliated marble and quartzite
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is the strong distractor because it correctly pairs shale→gneiss and limestone→marble but swaps sandstone and coal products, which are the less-commonly memorized transformations.
elimination_logic: Shale → high-grade metamorphism → gneiss (via slate, phyllite, schist sequence) — pair A-3.
Limestone → marble (non-foliated, calcite recrystallization) — pair B-1.
Sandstone → quartzite (non-foliated, quartz recrystallization) — pair C-4.
Coal → graphite (maximum coalification/metamorphism) — pair D-2, confirming option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits uncertainty about the coal → graphite transformation and the sandstone → quartzite pairing. Students who know limestone → marble and shale → gneiss (the two most frequently taught pairs) but are unsure about sandstone and coal metamorphic products will make entity-swap errors in List II. Sandstone → quartzite and coal → graphite are less-drilled pairs, making them the critical discriminators in this match-the-column question.
solution.final_explanation:
Metamorphic transformation is protolith-specific — composition determines the product. These four pairs represent the most examination-relevant protolith-product relationships.

| Protolith | Metamorphic Product |
|---|---|
| Shale | Gneiss (high-grade) via slate→phyllite→schist→gneiss |
| Limestone | Marble (non-foliated, calcite recrystallization) |
| Sandstone | Quartzite (non-foliated, quartz recrystallization) |
| Coal | Graphite (extreme metamorphism) |

• A-3 (Shale → Gneiss): Shale is the classic pelitic protolith; progressive metamorphism through Barrovian zones produces gneiss at the highest grade.
• B-1 (Limestone → Marble): Calcite recrystallizes; non-foliated because calcite does not form platy minerals. Makrana marble (Taj Mahal) is India's iconic example.
• C-4 (Sandstone → Quartzite): Quartz grains fuse under heat/pressure; non-foliated because quartz does not align under stress like sheet silicates.
• D-2 (Coal → Graphite): Intense metamorphism of carbon-rich coal converts it to graphite — hexagonally layered pure carbon.

Value Addition:
• Quartzite is harder than sandstone — quartz-quartz fusion eliminates weak cement planes.
• Marble's lack of foliation makes it easier to carve — prized in sculpture and architecture.
• Ultra-high pressure metamorphism (coesite, microdiamonds in gneiss) records subduction to mantle depths.

solution.concept_anchor: Petroleum in sedimentary basins — porous sandstone/limestone reservoirs

statement_analysis.statement: Petroleum and natural gas are generated from the thermal maturation of organic matter preserved in sedimentary source rocks, and they migrate into porous reservoir rocks such as sandstone and limestone.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately describes the petroleum system: organic matter (kerogen) in shale source rocks is heated during burial, generating hydrocarbons that migrate upward into porous and permeable reservoir rocks (sandstone, limestone) where they are trapped by impermeable cap rocks.

statement_analysis.statement: Coal deposits in India's Gondwana sequences provide the primary source of petroleum for the country's refinery sector, as coal is chemically converted to liquid fuels through natural geological processes.
statement_analysis.reason: Coal is not the source of petroleum. Petroleum derives from marine organic matter (algae, zooplankton) in sedimentary basins. Coal forms from terrestrial plant matter and is used directly as a solid fuel — not converted to liquid petroleum by geological processes naturally. Coal-to-liquid (CTL) technology exists industrially but is not a natural geological process.

statement_analysis.statement: The Law of Superposition holds that in an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary strata, older rock layers are found below younger layers, allowing relative age determination of fossils.
statement_analysis.reason: Steno's Law of Superposition is a foundational stratigraphic principle — undisturbed sedimentary sequences have the oldest material at the base and youngest at the top, enabling relative dating of fossils and geological events.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Statement 1 NOT correct) is the strong distractor because students uncertain about the petroleum migration mechanism may question Statement 1, not realising it is a fully accurate description of the petroleum system.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: petroleum = thermal maturation of organic matter in shale source rocks → migration to sandstone/limestone reservoir rocks — correct, NOT the answer.

Scrutinize Statement 2: coal as source of petroleum is categorically false — petroleum comes from marine organic matter, not coal/terrestrial plant matter; natural geological processes do not convert coal to liquid petroleum.
Verify Statement 3: Law of Superposition = older strata below, younger above — foundational stratigraphy, correct, NOT the answer.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct → answer is (b) 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the association between 'carbon-based fossil fuels' and 'coal deposits in India.' Students who know coal and petroleum are both carbon-based fossil fuels found in sedimentary sequences may not distinguish their separate organic origins. Petroleum derives from marine planktonic organisms (marine source rocks — predominantly shale); coal derives from terrestrial plant matter accumulated in swampy environments. These are geologically distinct organic feedstocks with entirely different diagenetic/catagenetic pathways.
solution.final_explanation:
Fossil fuels differ fundamentally in their organic source material, even though both are products of organic matter in sedimentary basins.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Petroleum generation involves the burial and thermal transformation of marine-derived organic matter (kerogen Type I/II in shale source rocks) into oil and gas. Migration into porous reservoir rocks (sandstone, limestone) and trapping beneath impermeable cap rocks (shale, evaporite) constitutes the petroleum system.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Coal is NOT a source of petroleum. Coal forms from terrestrial plant debris and is a solid carbonaceous fuel. Petroleum derives from marine planktonic organisms. While industrial CTL (coal-to-liquid) technology exists, no natural geological process converts Gondwana coal to liquid petroleum.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Steno's Law of Superposition enables relative dating — the youngest stratum overlies the oldest in undisturbed sequences, allowing biostratigraphic correlation using index fossils.

Value Addition:
• India's major petroleum basins: Mumbai Offshore (Bombay High), Krishna-Godavari basin, Cambay basin — all sedimentary.
• Kerogen is the insoluble organic precursor in source rocks; it transforms to oil (Type I/II kerogen) or gas (Type III kerogen from terrestrial material) with increasing burial temperature.
• Source rock + reservoir rock + cap rock + trap structure = the four elements of a petroleum system.

solution.concept_anchor: Black cotton soil from basalt weathering — montmorillonite — agricultural significance
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is the strong distractor because both A and R are correct and students who recall 'basalt weathers to black cotton soil' may assume the relationship is fully and directly causal without examining whether R precisely explains A's agricultural significance.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? Yes — black cotton soil (Regur) is associated with the Deccan Plateau, formed by basalt weathering, and is highly suitable for rain-fed cotton cultivation due to its water-retention capacity.
Step 2: Is R correct? Yes — basalt is rich in calcium, magnesium, and iron; its weathering does produce montmorillonite (smectite) clay with high water-holding capacity.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? Yes — the high montmorillonite clay content (derived from basalt weathering) is precisely the cause of the soil's water-retention capacity, which makes it suitable for cotton in rain-fed areas where moisture retention between rains is critical.
Both A and R correct, R causally explains A → correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in this assertion-reason question is designed to test whether students can correctly identify a genuine causal relationship — as opposed to the more commonly tested 'both correct but R does not explain A' pattern. Here, R IS the correct explanation: montmorillonite clay's swelling-shrinking behavior and high water retention are precisely what make Regur soil suitable for rain-fed cotton (option a). Students trained to default to option (b) when both statements seem correct will be misled.
solution.final_explanation:
Black cotton soil (Regur) is the most agriculturally significant soil type in the Deccan Plateau, directly linked to the weathering of Deccan basalt.

• Assertion (A): Correct. Regur soil covers Maharashtra, Gujarat, MP, and parts of Andhra Pradesh — the prime cotton-growing belt. Its ability to retain moisture between rain events makes it ideal for rain-fed cotton cultivation in regions with seasonal rainfall.
• Reason (R): Correct. Basalt is a mafic rock rich in calcium, magnesium, iron, and silica. Its chemical weathering under humid tropical conditions produces montmorillonite (smectite) clay — a 2:1 clay mineral with an expanding lattice structure that gives the soil exceptional water retention and swelling capacity.
• Causal link: R directly and completely explains A. The montmorillonite clay content derived from basalt weathering IS the specific mechanism responsible for the high water-retention capacity that makes Regur suited for cotton. This is a genuine A←R causal relationship.

Value Addition:
• Regur soil cracks deeply in summer (shrinks when dry) and swells when wet — this 'self-plowing' action churns the subsoil, reducing the need for tillage.
• Montmorillonite (smectite) clay also causes engineering problems — expansive soils crack building foundations.
• The Deccan Trap basalt is the sole parent material for Regur — geographically, its distribution maps almost perfectly onto the Deccan basalt outcrop area.

solution.concept_anchor: Igneous rock properties — texture, composition, landform associations

statement_analysis.statement: Columnar jointing, as observed at natural sites like Giant's Causeway (Northern Ireland), is a feature produced when basalt contracts uniformly during cooling, forming hexagonal columns perpendicular to the cooling surface.
statement_analysis.reason: Columnar jointing in basalt results from thermal contraction — as the lava cools from the surface, tension cracks propagate perpendicular to the cooling surface, producing characteristic hexagonal columns. Giant's Causeway is the world's most cited example.

statement_analysis.statement: Obsidian is a fine-grained extrusive igneous rock with a well-developed crystal lattice, formed when silica-rich magma cools slowly enough to allow mineral crystallization.
statement_analysis.reason: Obsidian is a volcanic glass — it has NO crystal lattice. It forms when silica-rich (rhyolitic) magma cools so rapidly that there is no time for crystallization. The description of 'fine-grained with a crystal lattice' and 'slow cooling' contradicts obsidian's defining characteristics.

statement_analysis.statement: Porphyritic texture in igneous rocks — large crystals (phenocrysts) embedded in a finer matrix — indicates a two-stage cooling history where early slow cooling was followed by rapid cooling after magma reached the surface.
statement_analysis.reason: Porphyritic texture records two-stage cooling: initial slow cooling at depth allows phenocrysts to grow; subsequent eruption exposes the magma to rapid surface cooling, creating the fine-grained groundmass around the earlier-formed large crystals.

statement_analysis.statement: The Deccan Traps of India represent an intrusive igneous province where magma solidified at depth as a series of granite batholiths beneath the Deccan Plateau.
statement_analysis.reason: The Deccan Traps are an extrusive igneous province — specifically a flood basalt formation where lava erupted at the surface in successive flows. They are not batholiths, which are intrusive features. The composition is basaltic, not granitic.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (only three correct) is the strong distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are correct and Statement 4 is clearly wrong, but students unsure about obsidian's texture may accept Statement 2 as correct too, arriving at 'three correct' rather than 'two correct.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Columnar jointing in basalt from thermal contraction — correct.
Statement 2: Obsidian = volcanic GLASS, no crystal lattice, forms by rapid cooling — 'well-developed crystal lattice' and 'slow cooling' are both false — incorrect.
Statement 3: Porphyritic texture = two-stage cooling (slow underground + rapid at surface) — correct.
Statement 4: Deccan Traps = EXTRUSIVE basalt, not intrusive granite batholiths — incorrect.
Two statements correct (1, 3) → answer is (a) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits partial knowledge of obsidian — students know it is extrusive volcanic (correct) and associate 'fine-grained' with extrusive rocks (partially correct for other rocks) but forget that obsidian is specifically glassy (non-crystalline) and forms by extremely rapid cooling. The description of a 'crystal lattice' forming by 'slow cooling' is precisely opposite to obsidian's nature. Statement 4 is a straightforward intrusive/extrusive conflation of the Deccan Traps.
solution.final_explanation:
Igneous rock texture and landform associations test multi-dimensional knowledge of cooling rate, composition, and geological setting.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Basalt's uniform composition and contraction during cooling create perpendicular tension cracks that propagate as hexagonal columns. Giant's Causeway (~60 Ma Paleogene basalts of Northern Ireland) is the global reference; similar jointing occurs in Deccan basalt flows.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Obsidian is volcanic glass — it lacks any crystal structure. It forms from rhyolitic (high-silica) magma that quenches (chills instantaneously) on contact with water or air. 'Fine-grained' rock (e.g., basalt) has tiny crystals; obsidian has NO crystals — a critical distinction.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Porphyritic texture reflects magma that began cooling slowly (growing phenocrysts) then erupted and cooled rapidly (forming fine groundmass). Common in intermediate (andesitic) lavas of subduction zones.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Deccan Traps are extrusive flood basalts — lava flows at the surface. The word 'trap' comes from the stepped terrain formed by successive horizontal lava flows, not from batholithic intrusions. Deccan rocks are basaltic, not granitic.

Value Addition:
• Rhyolite is the extrusive equivalent of granite; basalt is the extrusive equivalent of gabbro.
• India has columnar basalt exposures in parts of Maharashtra and Karnataka within the Deccan Trap province.
• Porphyritic granite = 'rapakivi granite' — phenocrysts of orthoclase surrounded by plagioclase mantles — distinctive texture in ancient Proterozoic cratons.
